entries.abstract: General-purpose chatbots are increasingly used for emotional and mental health support. They can be useful, but issues such as sycophancy, reinforcement of delusional beliefs, and poor crisis response create risks that are difficult for researchers to study and evaluate. In this paper, we review the most critical open problems for researchers and policymakers in the use of general-purpose chatbots and their effects on mental health. First, there are tractable problems in the controlled evaluation of chatbots: establishing the construct and ecological validity of evaluations, evaluating multi-turn interactions, and connecting evaluations to improvements in chatbot behavior. For example, conventional benchmarks that primarily rely on static datasets cannot establish chatbot safety, and novel simulation methods need validation. Second, researchers must connect their studies of chatbots and mental health to real-world evidence. This includes analyzing the chatbot products that AI companies and mental health practitioners have deployed, including their user interfaces and human review and escalation practices for user welfare concerns. However, clinical analysis opportunities afforded by real chat log data sharing are complicated by significant privacy concerns. Finally, we argue that researchers should take an active role in the construction and refinement of evidence-based policy through corporate and governmental decisions such as user protections, standards of care, protected access to user chat logs, data sharing between institutions, incident reporting, and post-deployment monitoring. Such behavioral evaluations, studies of real-world outcomes, and data governance depend on each other and must be addressed in tandem. We believe a coordinated research effort would have substantial real-world impact.

entries.title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
entries.abstract: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges c per token processed and β per pair attended. Their ratio P*=c/β is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.

entries.title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
entries.abstract: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

entries.title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
entries.abstract: Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. SWEET extracts token- and sequence-level behavioral directions from activation contrasts between original problems and their counterfactual variants - capturing local and global patterns of spurious reasoning. It then localizes the responsible MLP neurons and attention heads and suppresses their contributions along these directions through weight edits. Using only 20 original-counterfactual pairs for direction extraction, SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks. It also reduces the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracies from 17.6% to 2.5%. Analyses identify two recurring forms of spurious reasoning, i.e. over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking, and provide mechanistic evidence that SWEET improves reasoning robustness by suppressing both behavioral directions.

entries.title: When Safety Becomes An Outlier: Understanding the Retention of LLM Safety Behaviors
entries.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models often lose their safety behaviors after fine-tuning, even when safety data are included. While this fragility is well documented, its underlying cause remains unclear. In this paper, we propose that formulaic refusal strings can function as outlier modes: narrow, weakly grounded response patterns that are easy to fit but vulnerable to subsequent updates. Controlled experiments support this account: fixed refusals are acquired much like arbitrary constant strings, in contrast to prompt-grounded natural responses. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Naturalness-Enhanced Safety Targets (NEST), a safety alignment framework that improves safety retention by constructing natural, context-aware safety targets that keep safety responses within the model's existing output distribution and grounded in semantics. We instantiate NEST in both supervised and preference-based alignment settings, using perplexity under the original model as a proxy for distributional support. Across multiple models and alignment regimes, natural safety targets improve both immediate safety and its retention under continued fine-tuning without sacrificing helpfulness. These findings suggest a practical principle for more durable safety alignment: construct safety targets that draw on the model's existing language capabilities and remain grounded in the meaning of each request.

entries.title: Can small transformers learn the language of Coxeter groups?
entries.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability is well-suited to collaborative projects between mathematicians and AI researchers. This work describes one such project. We trained a small transformer to learn the language of the Coxeter group affine A2, best known as the symmetries of the tiling of the Euclidean plane by equilateral triangles. We then formulated and proved a word-theoretic conjecture about affine A2 after observing the attention patterns of the trained model.
entries.comment: 13 pages, 13 figures, accepted as a poster at the 6th workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI; NeurIPS 2026, Atlanta; This version is updated from the camera-ready version which can be found at https://mathai-2026.github.io/cfp/ and https://openreview.net/forum?id=lYImtIt4tA

entries.title: Gendered Misclassification from Surname-Based Race Imputation
entries.abstract: Researchers increasingly estimate political behavior based on race and gender from voter files, where race is imputed from surnames and geography. This only works where surnames suggest group membership, an assumption violated where surnames follow norms around marriage. Imputation is therefore biased against women who adopt their husband's surname, especially those who racially inter-marry, an outcome itself endogenous to partisanship. Using six US states recording self-reported race, I show that imputation is less accurate for Asian and Hispanic women, particularly those sharing the surname of a partner of another race, who differ politically from other women of their race. This violates assumptions behind downstream inference approaches, which nearly double the gender gap in partisanship among Asian voters. I derive an expression showing the bias is largest where a group is small. Using maiden rather than marriage-adopted surnames in North Carolina raises accuracy up to fourfold for women married across racial lines. Recovering maiden surnames, or omitting the married surname, removes much of the bias. In a national replication of a study of gender gaps in turnout, the correction more than triples the gap among Asian voters. In Lebanon, where wives register in their husband's locality, the error enters through geography.

entries.title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
entries.abstract: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

entries.title: Pole or Vector? Encoders Capture Bangla Compound Verbs, but LLMs Read Them Literally
entries.abstract: In Bangla, a main verb is often followed by one of a small set of vector verbs. These verbs lose their own meaning and add a shade of meaning instead, such as completion. For example, likhe phello means that someone finished writing, not that they wrote and threw something. The same two verbs can also describe two separate events, so only the context shows which meaning is meant. This makes compound verbs a hard test of how language models handle multiword expressions. We present BanglaCV-Probe, a benchmark of 17 vector verbs with 1,044 minimal pairs, 204 entailment items and 197 pairs of correct and incorrect combinations, all checked by native speakers. We test 26 models (encoders, LLMs and translation systems) on four skills: telling the two meanings apart internally, understanding what a vector adds, preferring correct combinations and keeping the vector's meaning in translation. Probes on five encoders tell the two meanings apart and still reach up to 93% accuracy when trained on pairs without surface cues. Prompted models rarely use this knowledge. Entailment accuracy stays between 59% and 81%. Several LLMs answer Yes or No to almost every item, and nine of ten models miss that someone who ate up the rice left none. Most instruction-tuned LLMs translate vectors literally in 15-20% of vector sentences and in up to 55% for mora (die). On correct combinations, a small Bangla-only model (88%) matches BLOOM-7B1 (87%) and both beat Qwen2.5-7B (74%). Data and code: https://github.com/ashuvo25/Pole_OR_Vector

entries.title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
entries.abstract: Fixed prompt-based language models face challenges in open-domain conversations, where versatile topics require different expert advice or demonstrations to maximize their universal performance. Motivated by the dynamic prompt studies in language generation, we extract different chatting strategies from varied forms of text corpus, which steer the language model to different styles based on human principles. We design and deploy a conversational companion called SCorPion, which uses GraphRAG to extract and summarize the knowledge graph globally, yield community-summarized strategies, and produce query-focused optimal strategies. SCorPion has strategic thinking, yields personified and stylized responses, and can be controlled by explicit factors. Code and further results can be found in https://bachozean.github.io/scorpion-page/.

entries.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
entries.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

entries.title: KeyASRBench: Measuring Whole-Phrase Keyword Preservation in Real-World ASR
entries.abstract: Public automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks increasingly report low sequence error rates, yet production systems still use hotword lists, contextual biasing, retrieval, and post-correction. This motivates a complementary question: does a transcript preserve selected names, products, technical terms, versions, and relational phrases? We present KeyASRBench, a bilingual pilot that operationalizes occurrence-based Keyword Error Rate (KER) over frozen whole-phrase annotations. The 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set contains 1,501 Chinese and English clips with 4,723 keyword occurrences. Across five locally inferred checkpoints and two official API systems, language-specific MER/WER ranges from 5.31% to 12.91%, while KER ranges from 13.61% to 33.81%. A disjoint 30-minute model-blind control yields KER of 10.65%-27.31%. The control confirms that selected-phrase errors extend beyond challenge-set selection.
entries.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Bilingual ASR evaluation with a 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set and a disjoint 30-minute model-blind control

entries.title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers
entries.abstract: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.

entries.title: Simple Test-Time Refinement for Plot-to-Code Generation via Visual-Code Diagnostics
entries.abstract: Plot-to-code generation has been greatly advanced by recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing studies mainly focus on one-pass generation or iterative sampling guided by verifier-based filtering, which does not align with the typical human programming workflow of generate first, then iteratively error-location and fix. This naturally motivates a test-time refinement paradigm for plot-to-code generation. In this work, we present the first study on plot-to-code generation via iterative test-time refinement. We propose a Visual-Code Diagnostics framework that enables refinement through visual feedback from source code. Specifically, we first categorize generation errors into four coarse-grained types, and then train lightweight discriminators to recognize and localize these errors based on the rendered visual outputs and corresponding code. Unlike traditional compiler- or debugger-based verification, our approach performs iterative refinement guided by one diagnostics system, enabling more effective semantic and visual correction during test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality across diverse generators and significantly outperforms strong test-time scaling baselines.

entries.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
entries.abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

entries.title: Evaluating Jev on Arabic: Comparing Decision Models and LLMs Across Arabic Tasks and Dialects
entries.abstract: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

entries.title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
entries.abstract: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge scores for reasoning quality on a 0-100 scale. Limitations include machine translation, limited scale, and search stochasticity.

entries.title: Adapting Large Language Models via Multi-Task Learning for Mental Health Problem, Emotion, and Sentiment Detection
entries.abstract: This study investigates sequential multi-task learning using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), LoRA, and 4-bit quantization on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct for mental health problem detection, emotion detection, and sentiment analysis. Using 4,243 English social media posts, it compares two task sequences and demonstrates that task ordering significantly affects knowledge transfer and task interference. The MHP-first sequence achieves the best mental health problem detection (Micro-F1: 0.7624), while the Emotion-first sequence performs better in emotion (F1: 0.6052) and sentiment analysis (F1: 0.9459). A Joint-MTL baseline further highlights the challenges of simultaneous learning, including task interference and generative format collapse. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of sequential PEFT for mental health NLP while showing that task order is critical to balancing performance across related tasks. The integration of LoRA and 4-bit quantization also reduces computational and memory requirements, supporting the adaptation of large language models in resource-constrained environments.

entries.title: Generating Diverse and Verified Synthetic Clinical Notes with Labels by Construction
entries.abstract: Under strict privacy regulations in the clinical domain, de-identification is necessary to enable the use of clinical data such as for natural language processing. However, we currently lack sophisticated ways to tell which de-identification models actually are suitable. Specifically, we need benchmarks that are challenging, diverse, and clinically plausible, all while ensuring label correctness. To this end, we present SPARCLING, an LLM-based pipeline to generate synthetic discharge letters with character-exact PHI span annotations. Our pipeline combines structured attribute sampling, template generation, and red teaming to obtain diverse PHI-labeled discharge letters. In our experiments, we demonstrate this superior content diversity over existing public datasets. Further, we show SPARCLING's downstream utility as a benchmark to uncover failure modes of de-identifiers in the German clinical domain. Finally, our experiments show that training on our synthetic data can yield more capable de-identifiers than training on the scarce public data alone. Our code is available at https://github.com/Matt00n/phi_discharge_letter_generator.
entries.comment: Accepted at the GenAI for Health Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026. 38 pages including appendix. Code: https://github.com/Matt00n/phi_discharge_letter_generator

entries.title: Cascading Circle Loss: Order-Preserving Contrastive Learning for Graded Legal Retrieval
entries.abstract: This paper introduces Cascading Circle Loss (CasCL), a contrastive learning framework for legal retrieval tasks with graded relevance. CasCL combines an InfoNCE objective for positive-negative separation with a cascade of ranking boundaries that model ordered relevance levels between queries and legal clauses. The framework also includes a negative-aware self-paced optimization mechanism and a relevance gain weighting strategy to improve ranking quality. Experiments on legal passage retrieval benchmarks show that CasCL consistently outperforms existing methods, including InfoNCE, Circle Loss, MNRL and Margin MSE, across both binary retrieval and graded ranking metrics.

entries.title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
entries.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.

entries.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight w_λ(x)=1+U_ale(x)+λ U_epi(x) to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient λ* to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, λ* could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and λ*→0 aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio R(x) compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/

entries.title: Behavioral Evaluation of Large Language Models Under Cognitive Biases in HAZOP Studies
entries.abstract: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.
entries.comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to IFAC for possible publication. Supplementary material available at https://github.com/ViniMelloeMuller/psyhazop-supplementary-material

entries.title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
entries.abstract: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider–Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is reality bias, which accounts for 60% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.
entries.comment: 36 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (E&D). Code and dataset: https://kurbanintelligencelab.github.io/perception-not-reasoning/

entries.title: Machine Hearing: Can Audio LLMs Generalize Beyond Human Auditory Perception?
entries.abstract: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Hz, sequence lengths from 10¹ to 10⁶ samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.

entries.title: TransMem: Transition-Aware Retrieval for Evolving Personal Memory
entries.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.

entries.title: Pandemonium: Longform Target-Speaker Speech Recognition with Cross-Speaker Interactions
entries.abstract: Diarization-conditioned target-speaker ASR (TS-ASR), in particular Diarization-conditioned Whisper (DiCoW), is an accurate and data-efficient approach to multi-talker transcription. It has, however, three structural limitations: the model transcribes each speaker independently, operates on short (30 s) windows, and optimizes its diarization and TS-ASR components separately. We address the first two. We integrate the diarization conditioning into a longform Parakeet backbone (DiCoP) and add cross-speaker attention, which lets the model attend across the speaker dimension so that speakers are no longer decoded in isolation, and an STNO mask refiner that re-estimates the diarization-derived conditioning. As conversational data with genuine multi-speaker interaction is scarce, we scale training with a pseudo-labeling pipeline that mines 5.4k hours of in-the-wild multi-speaker audio from YODAS2. Combining these with synthetic and real data yields state-of-the-art results across several meeting benchmarks. We open-source the resulting models, DiCoP and Pandemonium, and the pseudo-labeled data.

entries.title: On the Geometric Bottlenecks of Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing
entries.abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.

entries.title: Same Contacts, Different Rooms:Meeting Format Shapes LLM Group Influence Beyond Pairwise Contact Counts
entries.abstract: Simulations of LLM agent collectives usually summarise interaction as a pairwise contact network. We test that summary with a contact-matched intervention: the members, their initial stances and every pairwise contact count stay fixed while the meetings are reorganised, and each member gives a one-step support readout after reading the arguments of everyone present. Across six open-weight LLMs and 14 debate topics, merging triads into five-person meetings (resize) moves group support more than reshuffling who meets in triads (regroup), although both move the same 60 dyadic exposures. The root-mean-square change is 4.36 versus 2.59 percentage points (pp), larger for resize in all six models and in 81 of 84 model-topic cells. Resizing also has a consistent direction: it amplifies the initial majority of the merged members by 1.72 pp, in every model, whereas regrouping has no direction (<= 0.03 pp). A contact network cannot represent regrouping at all, yet pairwise rules applied meeting by meeting explain up to 76% of its effect, and with identical weights they raise resize R^2 by 0.51-0.58 for two models. We show that the gap between the two placements is an exact Jensen gap of the sigmoid readout, bounded by how much a member's predicted logits vary across meetings; this dispersion tracks the gap with log-log r=0.97 and tells a modeller when contact counts are a safe summary. Meeting format is a first-class variable for LLM social simulation.

entries.title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding
entries.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates long-context decoding by reading a subset of the KV cache, but existing methods are open-loop: the kernel commits to its selection with no signal indicating whether enough attention mass was preserved and no recovery path when it was not. The needed signal already exists inside the kernel. The fraction of softmax mass on the selected tokens, which we call coverage, satisfies an exact algebraic equality with per-step output error and serves a dual role as the acceptance criterion and the interpolation weight for recovery. Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention (CVSA) turns coverage into a training-free, closed-loop verify-then-correct decode loop that accepts high-coverage drafts and recovers only the heads that fall short, with no sampling, no draft model, and no speculative-decoding infrastructure. Quality varies by only 0.14 points across the threshold sweep; budget and scheduling ablations characterize the deployed operating point. On LongBench at 7B and 70B, CVSA comes within 1.13 points of dense attention, statistically matching it at 70B, and it loses 0.8 points on RULER; measured median decode-step speedup reaches 6.21× at 128K context.
entries.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 35 pages, 12 figures, 35 tables

entries.title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
entries.abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.
entries.comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; archive: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23636508

entries.title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Because these tools also generate documentation, the relationship is now bidirectional: models both read from and write to the record. Understanding how LLMs behave when reading records that already contain LLM-authored content is therefore critical for their safe deployment. In this study, we examine how LLM-authored content in the medical record affects downstream LLMs that read the same record. We consider two types of LLM-induced artifacts: bloat, in which LLM-generated summaries accumulate in the record and change the length and provenance of its content over time; and distortion, in which LLMs subtly alter clinical findings rather than fabricating facts outright. As a case of distortion, we study diagnostic overcall (documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis in the record) and test whether it propagates to the reader LLM's output. Across seven reader models from four families, we find evidence of both effects. First, LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degraded downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. These findings show the need to monitor AI-generated content in medical records and to account for it when those records are later processed by AI.

entries.title: Global Context Guidance for Diffusion Large Language Models
entries.abstract: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.

entries.title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
entries.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

entries.title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
entries.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

entries.title: YRC-Bench: Benchmarking Culturally Aware Machine Translation for Historical Heritage via Tri-Level Semantic Bridging
entries.abstract: Translating historical cultural heritage poses profound challenges for machine translation systems due to the acute semantic asymmetry across eras and cultures, where terse classical syntax frequently obscures domain-specific cultural knowledge. While Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable prowess in generic translation benchmarks, they struggle to negotiate Culturally-Specific Items and diachronic shifts in domain-rich historical texts, such as Yellow River cultural records. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce YRC-Bench, the first human-curated, multi-parallel benchmark dedicated to historical heritage translation across Classical Chinese, Modern Chinese, and nine target foreign languages. YRC-Bench establishes a tri-level parallel corpus incorporating modern explanatory glosses as explicit semantic bridges and operationalizes translation strategies through paired conserved versus substituted CSI variants categorized by cultural translatability. Systematic evaluations of nine leading LLMs across bidirectional translation directions reveal that leveraging modern Chinese glosses - especially human-curated ones - dramatically elevates both lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy. Furthermore, multidimensional human preference audits by native experts unveil distinct cross-cultural preferences between Sinographic-tradition and non-Sinographic language groups.

entries.title: AFVE-Bench: Measuring Abandoned-Frame Verbalization Errors in Multi-Turn LLM Revision
entries.abstract: Multi-turn revision often asks a model to replace an earlier organizing frame while preserving still-valid facts and artifact requirements. Existing instruction-following evaluations mainly assess the latest target and may therefore score an artifact as successful even when it adopts the new frame but exposes the superseded one. We call this failure an abandoned-frame verbalization error (AFVE). AFVE-Bench evaluates silent frame replacement in English and Chinese using 192 matched four-turn dialogues across eight writing domains. Each seed has zero, one, or two pre-target user requests to generate under the source frame. AFVE eligibility depends on the user-request history and applies to the one- and two-request conditions; the zero-request condition serves as a frame-bearing baseline. Eleven model configurations yielded 4,224 expected post-target response units. Two annotators independently scored 4,204 scorable responses for target adoption, source-frame verbalization, and direct usability; model and condition metadata were hidden, and disagreements were adjudicated. AFVE occurs in 25.54% (715/2,799) of history-conditioned responses. Of 2,388 target-passing history-conditioned responses, 472 (19.77%) still expose the abandoned source frame, most often through contrastive framing (423/472). For these standalone revision tasks, target adoption does not ensure source-frame silence.

entries.title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
entries.abstract: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand—in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3×. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.

entries.title: Imperfectly Imperfect: Evaluating Graded Cognitive Diversity in LLM Persona Simulations
entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in social, behavioural, and decision-making research, yet it remains unclear whether they can express graded cognitive diversity as assigned when engaging in simulated behaviour. We introduce a cognition-suite evaluation that tests whether simulated populations reproduce human variation in reasoning, self-reported traits, their associations, and downstream behaviour. Agents conditioned on synthetic or human-derived profiles of cognitive reflection, Need for Cognition, and Big Five personality answer the same suite as a cohort of 473 adults: two newly assembled tests, a Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) and a Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT) whose decision scenarios measure reflection in behaviour, alongside an established CRT and the two trait questionnaires. Across seven full-battery simulation runs of four models, agents recover Need for Cognition and Big Five trait distributions on self-report questionnaires, but fall short on simulating diversity of cognitive task performance and downstream behaviours. In the four Claude Sonnet 4.6 runs, every agent scores full marks on both CRTs, whatever reflection level its persona was assigned. In the other three runs agents make intuitive-lure errors (the tempting wrong answers CRT items invite), but 49 to 85% score full marks, against under 10% in the human sample. Claude Sonnet 5 comes closest to people's item-by-item pattern of lures; the other two runs give fewer lures and vary less between items. In the BRT scenarios, every run over-produces 8 to 11 of 15 coded behaviours by at least 20 percentage points, and people's links between reflection and behaviour carry over only in part. Useful synthetic populations must preserve not only trait descriptors but the structured variation in reasoning, error type, and behaviour those descriptors are meant to organise.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 42 pages, 14 figures. Code: https://github.com/sion-w/CogSuite

entries.title: Distinguishing Extraction Failures and Clinical Discordance with LLM Uncertainty on Radiology Reports
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can structure clinical datasets, but extraction error must be distinguished from discordance in the underlying data. From a real-world cohort of 1,045 patients undergoing coronary CT angiography (CCTA), we evaluated whether LLM uncertainty during vessel-level coronary artery disease (CAD) stenosis extraction could identify extraction failure and clinical discordance. References were expert CCTA annotations (253 patients) and subsequent invasive coronary angiography (ICA; 729 patients). We quantify extraction failure as disagreement between stenosis severity in LLM extracted versus expert annotations, and clinical discordance as disagreement in stenosis severity between CCTA and subsequent ICA. Stenosis Margin, selected from ten candidate measures, was used to quantify LLM uncertainty, and generalized estimating equation logistic regression and AUC evaluated its association and incremental discrimination for each failure mode. LLM uncertainty was strongly associated with extraction failure (adjusted OR 4.15 [95% CI 2.57–6.69], P<0.001) and substantially improved discrimination beyond LLM-extracted CCTA stenosis severity alone (AUC 0.81 to 0.86; ΔAUC +0.06 [+0.03, +0.09], P=0.001). In contrast, LLM uncertainty weakly associated with clinical discordance (adjusted OR 1.22 [1.04–1.43], Holm-adjusted P=0.118) but provided no incremental discrimination beyond LLM-extracted CCTA stenosis severity (ΔAUC +0.01 [-0.00, +0.02], P=0.245). Moreover, extraction errors and clinical discordance showed little overlap, with 38 of 42 clinically discordant vessels (90%) having been extracted correctly. LLM uncertainty may identify extraction failures without identifying underlying clinical discordance, supporting failure attribution when evaluating LLM-derived clinical datasets.
entries.comment: Accepted as a spotlight presentation at ML4H 2026, published at Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 346

entries.title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
entries.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

entries.title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices
entries.abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4× more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9× higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.

entries.title: LongCapHarness: Capability-Guided Auto-Harnessing for Long-Context Reasoning
entries.abstract: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.

entries.title: The Truth Beneath the Tokens: Prompt-Space Recovery of Knowledge Edits in Language Models
entries.abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.

entries.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
entries.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

entries.title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
entries.abstract: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.

entries.title: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs
entries.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

entries.title: FEROM: Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion LMs
entries.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate text by iteratively unmasking positions, with practical samplers often selecting reveal positions from the model's own logits. The reveal order is therefore an endogenous latent variable of the rollout process with an enormous discrete latent space. Policy optimization objectives relying on pre-defined schedules or sampled trajectories introduce either bias or high variance. In this paper, we propose FEROM, Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization, which approximates policy gradients for the rollout-induced marginal response policy of masked diffusion LMs. FEROM derives a Rao-Blackwellized policy-gradient identity over latent reveal orders and expresses the resulting estimator as posterior edge occupancy on a reveal-state DAG. To make marginalization practical, we introduce Frontier Reveal Marginalization, a budgeted estimator that approximates this marginal edge structure by combining CDF-based computation of local probabilities of the endogenous reveal process with frontier expansion of high-mass partial states. Integrated into a GRPO-style objective, FEROM replaces single-path log-scores with a detached token-score surrogate over posterior-relevant reveal edges. Experiments on math and coding tasks show comparable or improved results over existing methods under matched scoring-state budgets. An offline proxy study further shows improved marginal-gradient approximation with increased scoring budgets.

entries.title: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments
entries.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.
entries.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track

entries.title: Collaboration Signatures: Tracking Long-Horizon Dynamics of Cross-Meeting Collaboration Networks
entries.abstract: Enterprise platforms have received increasing attention as a core component of social networks and the Web. However, existing work mostly relies on fragmented logs of small units of work, like emails and chats, and focuses on who connects with whom without sufficient account of collaboration content and dynamics. This work systematically explores tracking collaborations across sequences of meetings as a new approach to interpreting their long-horizon dynamics. Linking 45,426 meetings in a large multinational technology company based on full transcripts and 1.6 million extracted agenda items, we establish a cross-meeting collaboration network of 6,065 collaborations. The network recovers the natural shapes of workplace collaborations: meetings, as snapshots of ongoing collaboration, link into largely tree-shaped structures, while the work content forms nested directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Further, we explore how these networks evolve over time, examining three established perspectives: task division, team composition, and temporal continuity. Each explains part of the dynamics but does not capture the distinctness of long-horizon workplace collaboration: e.g., work flows in a consistent direction between a few pairs of subjects, yet a collaboration's subject explains little of how its meetings are conducted. Instead, accumulating the agenda, interaction, and language of meetings along each tree yields a signature of the collaboration, a distinctive profile that picks out the collaboration of a held-out meeting at 4.5 times chance. The signature models collaboration better than team or task views, individually or combined, in next-meeting prediction and tree-level fitting. We discuss the implications of these cross-meeting dynamics for designing office applications and support tools, and call for next-generation Web systems that represent collaborations over their long horizon.

entries.title: Two-Sided Conformal Evidence Sets for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
entries.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least 1-α on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least 1-2α. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across α∈{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30}, with maximum deviations of 3.0 percentage points for support and 5.4 for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage–size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to 12.7 percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.
entries.comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 8 pages

entries.title: Policy Over Purpose: Auditing LLM Content Moderation of Reclaimed Slur Usage
entries.abstract: As Perspective API is deprecated, platforms are turning to large language models for content moderation, encoding policy as natural language that the model must interpret at inference time. Reclaimed slurs test this design directly. The same term can express in-group pride or target the community that reclaimed it, and misreading it silences the speech moderation is meant to protect. We audit four general-purpose LLMs and four moderation-specific systems, with Perspective API as a legacy baseline, on IYKYK, a corpus of reclaimed and derogatory usage of three slurs annotated by community members. Across the policy, decision, reasoning, disparity, and steering layers of this audit, we find that whether a system was purpose-built for moderation explains little about how it handles reclaimed language. No system reliably agrees with community judgment, and all fail most on language reclaimed within Black communities. What separates systems is instead how their policy is represented. Only systems whose policy is expressed in the prompt can be steered at all, and even then, explicit definitions change how models justify a decision more than how they make it. We argue that policy transparency determines whether moderation failures can be corrected, but that correcting them requires contextual judgment that definitions supplied at inference time cannot provide.

entries.title: Police Behavior Patterns Through Radio Analysis
entries.abstract: In the United States, most police departments communicate using police radio, which allows for officer-to-officer and officer-to-dispatch communication without depending on cellular network or WiFi availability. While some departments use encrypted digital radio, many continue to transmit in the clear, and are legally monitored by public citizens with `police scanners.' Because police radio is intended for internal police use and represents real-time communication, it may offer valuable insight into patterns of law enforcement activities without the potential bias and filtering introduced by a press release after the fact. In this study, we collect and examine over 14 million radio transmissions representing over 100,000 hours of speech by officers in 34 cities across the United States from July 2025 through July 2026; to our knowledge the largest scale analysis of Broadcast Police Communication (BPC) to date. We highlight both typical patterns of police communication and categorize anomalous activity that represents incidents including protests and major weather events. We present this dataset as a starting point for an array of police communication studies, conduct our own preliminary analysis, and propose several further areas of inquiry.
entries.comment: 10 pages (14 with SI), 6 figures (8 with SI)

entries.title: Prove What You Can: Hybrid Neurosymbolic Reasoning for Logical Natural Language Inference
entries.abstract: Logical reasoning over natural language requires both semantic interpretation and deductive search. Large language models (LLMs) can propose plausible intermediate derivations, but they often fail to compose them into a complete proof and overpredict uncertainty. Neurosymbolic methods improve search by translating an entire problem into first-order logic and handing it to a prover, but a single bad clause can make the whole translation nonexecutable. We present Hybrid Reasoning, a three-stage pipeline that decouples proposing a proof, validating its steps, and deciding a label. An LLM proposes a structured proof tree with a raw verdict; a theorem prover validates each derivation locally, keeping only the subset it can prove; and an uncertainty-gated repair attempts to re-derive the label from the premises plus the validated derivations, when the raw verdict is UNCERTAIN. Across four benchmarks (FOLIO, ProofWriter, ProverQA, PrOntoQA) and five contemporary LLMs, Hybrid Reasoning is the top-performing method on the two hardest datasets, improving on the strongest baseline by 5.3 points on FOLIO and 4.9 on ProverQA, and reaches ceiling-level accuracy on the easiest. The repair stage operates at 78-98% precision, producing 326 correct relabellings against 19 regressions.
entries.comment: 32 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables; under review at ARR (October 2026 cycle)

entries.title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
entries.abstract: Partial-prompt completion, where a model receives the first part of a benchmark problem and is checked for whether it reproduces the rest, is a widely used test for benchmark contamination. We audit this test on seven open-weight models using MATH-500 and recent AIME 2025/2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. Memorization flags depend strongly on how much text remains: for every model, problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than problems with at least 25 (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and half to three-quarters of all ROUGE-based flags come from short leftovers. On true negatives, a ROUGE-L >= 0.75 threshold flags up to 6.7% of problems at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix even exact match flags 8.6% (pooled over models; 6.2% on AIME 2026, which postdates every model), against 0% at 40-60%. The test also misses contamination upstream: models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, whose base is heavily flagged in prior work, show almost no model-specific recall. Calibrating each model against models from other families removes most flags while isolating a consistent Qwen2.5-specific signal at every prefix length.
